complexity_matrix.operation: Read or write one next / prev field
complexity_matrix.notes: A single dereference: address computed from a base register, then loaded. No arithmetic in N and no search, independent of list length.
Three pointer assignments and one allocation. O(1) regardless of N — the canonical constant-time mutation.
head = head->next followed by freeing the old node. Reaching the head is free.

complexity_matrix.operation: Delete at a node whose predecessor is already held
complexity_matrix.notes: Rewire prev->next around curr, then free curr. The search for prev is excluded because the caller supplies it.

complexity_matrix.operation: Delete at an unknown index k
complexity_matrix.notes: The only reason singly-linked deletion can be linear: locating the predecessor costs k edges. This is a search cost, not a mutation cost.

complexity_matrix.operation: Append with a maintained tail pointer
complexity_matrix.notes: tail->next = new; tail = new. Omitting the tail field silently degrades every append to O(N).

complexity_matrix.operation: Append without a maintained tail pointer
complexity_matrix.notes: Must walk the whole list to find the end. Same class as the sort-precondition problem: the structure is capable of O(1), the implementation is not.
Random access does not exist on a list; k edges must be followed. k = 0 is O(1) by convention.
Each of N nodes is visited once. In-place reversal needs only three pointers, so auxiliary space stays constant.
Bounded by tail length plus one cycle length. O(1) space where a hash set of seen nodes would cost O(N) space.
8 bytes of next pointer on 64-bit for a singly-linked node, 16 for a doubly-linked one, plus allocator bookkeeping per independent allocation.

complexity_matrix.operation: Cache misses during a sequential traversal
complexity_matrix.notes: Roughly one miss per node because allocations are scattered across the heap. Identical Theta(N) to a contiguous scan but an order of magnitude slower in wall-clock terms.

correctness_argument.claim: Every splice replaces a two-edge path prev -> curr -> curr->next with a single edge, so a walk from head visits exactly the same elements minus curr, and curr becomes unreachable and therefore safe to free. In reversal, saving next before overwriting curr->next is what prevents the untraversed suffix from being lost.

cost_derivations.claim: Pointer operations are O(1) because an address is computed rather than searched; every cost that depends on position is therefore the cost of locating that position, which is why append is O(1) with a tail pointer and O(N) without.

limits.claim: Unordered search admits no improvement on Omega(N), so faster lookup requires maintaining order, which a balanced tree buys at O(log N) per insertion. Contiguity cannot be recovered, which caps the practical advantage of any pointer-based design.
